title: One In 8,000

jokes.text: It's a long story, but the short version is, I'm currently catfishing Anthony Kiedis.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April how she got the Red Hot Chili Peppers to donate a signed guitar.
jokes.punchline: April casually reveals she is actively catfishing the lead singer of RHCP as a fundraising strategy.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect April joke. The 'long story / short version' structure sets up an expectation of something mundane, then the punchline is bizarre and specific — not just 'I know someone' but 'I am catfishing the actual lead singer.' The character integration is exceptional: only April would do this and deliver it with zero affect. Scores an 8.5 because it's genuinely exceptional but doesn't quite reach legendary status.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I told them I was dying and only had six months to live. They sent me a signed guitar, a handwritten note, and front row tickets to their next show.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not dying. I just really wanted that guitar.

jokes.text: ...if I'm gonna perform Islands In the Stream with a Sacagawea hologram.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining that the charity auction needs to raise money for the unity concert.
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions she plans to perform a Kenny Rogers/Dolly Parton duet with a hologram of the historical figure Sacagawea.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Leslie: her obsession with both Pawnee history and ambitious spectacle collide into one perfectly absurd sentence. The specificity of the song choice ('Islands In the Stream') and the historical figure (Sacagawea) elevates this above generic absurdism. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to raise money for the Parks Department, and I have the perfect idea. We'll have a charity auction where I duet with a hologram of a historical figure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's... that's not a real thing we can do.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude! I'm thinking me and Eleanor Roosevelt, doing a medley of showtunes. Or maybe Abraham Lincoln doing a rap battle.

jokes.text: I am not good at keeping secrets. That's exactly what I told Kyle when he told me his wife was cheating on him.
jokes.setup: Andy admits he's not good at keeping secrets.
jokes.punchline: He illustrates this by immediately revealing that Kyle's wife is cheating — proving the point in real time.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully self-demonstrating joke — Andy proves his own point by doing the exact thing he's describing, immediately. The meta-structure where the illustration of the flaw IS the flaw is tight writing. Strong character work for Andy. The 'Andy, come on!' reaction beat that follows amplifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Have you told anyone about the baby?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No! I haven't told a soul. I've been keeping it locked up tight. I haven't even told Ben, I haven't told my mom, I haven't told the squirrels outside my window who I talk to every morning.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is the hardest thing I've ever done. Harder than learning to read. Harder than the time I ate a whole wheel of cheese.

jokes.text: My neighbor Eric — he's kept a secret for 20 years. He's in Witness Protection.
jokes.setup: Andy is reassuring April he can keep a secret by citing an example of someone who succeeded.
jokes.punchline: His example of a secret-keeper is a man whose secret is only secret because he's in Witness Protection — defeating the entire argument.
jokes.explanation: A tight little two-beat joke. The setup promises a heartening example, but the reveal that the secret is 'Witness Protection' simultaneously reveals Eric's secret, proves Andy's point about himself (he even knows this), and is inherently absurd. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not good at keeping secrets.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, Ben told me he's actually bald and wears a toupee, and I just blurted it out!

jokes.text: Ron Swanson asking for help? [shouts loudly]
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson, the proudly self-sufficient libertarian, enters Donna's office to ask for a favor.
jokes.punchline: Donna screams in exaggerated disbelief, as if this is a historic impossibility.
jokes.explanation: Relies on well-established Ron characterization. The shout is a great physical escalation of what might otherwise be a simple line. Works because it's earned by seasons of Ron refusing help.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My neighbor Eric kept a secret for 20 years.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Turns out he's been a serial killer the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was like, 'Eric, dude, you could've just told me you didn't like me!'

jokes.text: Keep your voice down, woman!
jokes.setup: Donna shouts about Ron asking for a favor.
jokes.punchline: Ron's irritated, hushed command, as if the concept of him needing help is a shameful state secret.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and very Ron. The economy is excellent. Functions as a good tag to joke #6.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to ask you for a favor.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Ron Swanson asking for a favor? That's like seeing a unicorn made of wood.

jokes.text: Tammy two once seduced a coroner and had me declared legally dead just so she could get a discount on a plane ticket.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his tortured relationship history with his two ex-wives named Tammy, comparing them to Donna's problematic ex Joe.
jokes.punchline: The specific, escalating absurdity of seducing a coroner to get a plane ticket discount — the motive being the most mundane possible for such an elaborate crime.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The escalation is masterful: the setup suggests extreme behavior, then the punchline delivers the full absurdity (seducing a coroner), but the real kicker is the banality of the motive — a plane ticket discount. The contrast between the complexity of the scheme and the petty payoff is the comic engine. Highly quotable, only works as a Ron/Tammy lore joke, and is genuinely original. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor but more specific and surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Donna, I need your help with something.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: WHAT?! Ron Swanson needs HELP?!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Please keep your voice down. And yes, I... require assistance.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If you tell anyone about this, I will have you reassigned to the parks department in the Ramsett Park area.

jokes.text: I understand this problem well and agree to this exchange of services.
jokes.setup: Donna explains she needs Ron to keep Joe away from her, drawing the parallel to his Tammy problem.
jokes.punchline: Ron responds to a moment that calls for warmth or empathy with the formal language of a business transaction.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron joke — his emotional unavailability expressed through bureaucratic diction. 'Exchange of services' is a perfect choice. Works as a capper to the whole Donna/Joe setup scene.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Joe and I have a complicated relationship. It's like Ron and the government.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We're locked in an eternal struggle, neither of us will ever fully win, and we both secretly enjoy the conflict.

jokes.text: Maybe you should start taking it easy. You're stressing out for two now. / Hmm, that's actually a pretty decent t-shirt idea.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to get Leslie to slow down because she's pregnant, using the idiom 'eating for two' reframed as 'stressing for two.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response completely ignores the emotional content and pivots to evaluating it as a merchandising opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Tight double joke: Ben's witty reframe of 'eating for two' is good on its own, but Leslie's pivot to t-shirt monetization is the real punchline. Shows both characters perfectly — Ben being clever and caring, Leslie being unstoppably project-oriented.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy once drove forty miles out of her way to a different grocery store because they had a five-cent coupon on eggs.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Five cents. She spent three dollars in gas to save a nickel.

jokes.text: Someone say 'Saperstein'? Come on, you two. Let's saddle you up and put some jelly on the belly.
jokes.setup: Leslie casually mentions asking Dr. Saperstein for his opinion.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Saperstein appears immediately, as if he was listening — and his enthusiastic, slightly off-putting bedside manner ('saddle you up,' 'jelly on the belly') is played for comic discomfort.
jokes.explanation: Saperstein's entrance gag (appearing the moment his name is said) and his folksy, over-eager doctor phrasing ('jelly on the belly') establish his comic character efficiently. 'He's a little weird' from Ben is the perfect dry tag.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Joe makes me lose my mind. I can't think straight around him. My words get all jumbled up. I start sweating. My heart races. It's like my brain just stops working.

jokes.text: He's a little weird. / Mm-hmm.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein delivers his bizarre 'saddle you up' line and exits.
jokes.punchline: Ben and Leslie exchange a mutual, understated 'yep, that's weird' beat together.
jokes.explanation: A simple but effective mutual reaction beat. Functions as a good tag. Not remarkable on its own but serves the scene rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Donna, I need you to keep Joe away from me.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'll prepare a formal memo and file it in triplicate.

jokes.text: If you have a secret, you have to tell me. That's the whole point of marriage. You get twice the secrets.
jokes.setup: April catches Andy about to crack and pressures him to reveal the secret.
jokes.punchline: Her justification for being told is hilariously mercenary: marriage as a secret-aggregation pact, not an emotional partnership.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp April line. 'You get twice the secrets' reframes marriage through April's darkly transactional lens. It's funny because it's almost a logical argument — she's not wrong, exactly — but the framing strips all sentimentality from the institution. Great character voice. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I should ask Dr. Saperstein about this.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Did someone say Saperstein? I'm here to help with all your medical needs, from your love apples to your tummy banana.

jokes.text: I'm getting a picture of you volunteering at a public elementary school in case I ever need to blackmail you.
jokes.setup: Ron and Donna arrive at the elementary school; Ron is using a saw to help make costumes.
jokes.punchline: Donna's casual explanation for why she's photographing Ron reveals she has a long-game blackmail strategy as a hobby.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Donna joke. The reveal that she's preemptively gathering blackmail material on Ron is funny in itself, but 'in case I ever need to' implies this is a standard practice for her. Strong character integration for both Donna (scheming) and Ron (whose reputation is compromised by basic human decency).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Ben's dad is a little... unconventional.

jokes.text: Hello, Joe. My name is Ron Swanson. I am Donna's work-proximity associate.
jokes.setup: Joe warmly greets Donna. Ron introduces himself.
jokes.punchline: 'Work-proximity associate' — Ron refuses to use any word that implies friendship or social connection, even in a polite introduction.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. 'Work-proximity associate' is a coinage that perfectly encapsulates Ron's entire worldview and his refusal to acknowledge human connection. It is highly quotable, entirely specific to Ron, and structurally perfect — the setup of a normal introduction makes the deviation land harder. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality; the character integration and quotability push it above.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I forgot I had information on both hands.

jokes.text: I'm onto you, friend. / What? / Tread lightly.
jokes.setup: Joe is being perfectly pleasant and kind, saying 'don't hesitate to ask for anything.'
jokes.punchline: Ron, who has been warned that Joe is dangerous, responds to extreme friendliness with a menacing territorial warning.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of paranoid aggression directed at unearned niceness. Ron treating basic courtesy as a dangerous gambit is perfectly absurd. 'Tread lightly' is a great word choice — formal, ominous, absurd given the context of an elementary school volunteer event.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Married couples should share secrets. It's like a bank account. You deposit secrets, you withdraw secrets, you get interest on your secrets.

jokes.text: There is no reason for you not to be yourself. / [Laughs] I win. / It wasn't a competition.
jokes.setup: Ben and the doctor are ostensibly on the same side, but Leslie has framed the appointment as a referendum on whether she has to slow down.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Saperstein gives Leslie a clean bill of health to keep working; Leslie immediately and triumphantly declares victory over Ben.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's competitive framing of a prenatal appointment is very on-brand. 'I win' is a perfect Leslie beat. Ben's weary 'It wasn't a competition' is the ideal straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're acting weird about the secret.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not acting weird! Why would you say that? I'm totally normal. Everything is fine. Nothing is wrong.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: See, you're doing it right now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Doing what? I don't know what you're talking about.

jokes.text: The baby has two bodies?
jokes.setup: The doctor reveals there are two babies on the ultrasound.
jokes.punchline: Ben's stunned, literal interpretation ('the baby has two bodies?') captures the exact confused moment before comprehension arrives.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures the surreal moment of surprise and the lag between seeing and understanding. 'Two bodies' is a hilariously clinical way to process twins. Ben's confusion reads as both funny and endearing. Strong economy — five words doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm taking this photo of Ron for blackmail purposes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What? Donna, you can't just—

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I already did. And it's going in my files.

jokes.text: And here's a fourth. I'm so sorry, no. It's a little fleck of cream cheese on the screen.
jokes.setup: The audience has just absorbed triplets. The doctor appears to find a fourth baby.
jokes.punchline: It's cream cheese on the screen — both relieving the escalation tension and condemning the doctor as someone who eats breakfast at his ultrasound machine.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is a triple escalation: one baby → twins → triplets → apparent quadruplets (with the emotional terror that creates) → deflated by cream cheese. The cream cheese reveal does two things at once: it's a relief AND it's a damning character detail about the doctor. 'I'm so sorry, no' lands perfectly as his embarrassed pivot. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and clearly above it in structural sophistication.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm Ron Swanson. I don't believe in friendship. I like people just enough to not have to commit murder.

jokes.text: Wow, you guys really dodged a bullet. Can you imagine raising four children at one time? Ha, a nightmare.
jokes.setup: The doctor just revealed it was cream cheese not a fourth baby — Ben and Leslie are still processing triplets.
jokes.punchline: The doctor cheerfully suggests they 'dodged a bullet' by only having triplets, completely oblivious to the fact that triplets is still devastating news.
jokes.explanation: Great beat of oblivious perspective. The doctor's framing of triplets as the lucky outcome is darkly funny, and his enthusiasm ('Ha, a nightmare') for a scenario they are literally facing right now shows his complete lack of bedside manner. Works as a tag to the cream cheese joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't trust him. Something's not right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, he's just being nice.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly. Nobody is that nice. He's up to something.

jokes.text: We knocked it out of the park on the first try. If we do this right, we can be parents to 1/3 of the supreme court!
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have just received the triplets news and are processing it.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately frames three children as a strategic achievement, specifically calculating their probability of producing a Supreme Court justice.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Leslie: she turns a shocking personal moment into a policy/achievement framing within seconds. '1/3 of the supreme court' is specific enough to be funny (not 'they'll be great' but 'statistically, one will be a justice'). Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, there's two of them? How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Congratulations, you're having twins.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So Leslie's been cheating on me?

jokes.text: ...it's what we doctors like to call — and I don't mean to be insensitive — a going-out-of-business sale.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein is explaining that Leslie's age makes her prone to releasing multiple eggs.
jokes.punchline: He pre-empts his own insensitivity with a disclaimer, then delivers an absolutely brutal metaphor for a woman's declining fertility.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The 'I don't mean to be insensitive' disclaimer is a perfect structural device — it simultaneously signals he absolutely is going to be insensitive and makes the punchline hit harder by contrast. 'Going-out-of-business sale' is a genuinely original and memorable coinage. The economic metaphor for fertility is fresh, specific, and wickedly funny. Highly quotable. Comparable to or slightly above the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: It's just cream cheese on the screen

jokes.text: Leslie, I need you to be Buddha on quaaludes, and, Ben, you are Matthew McConaughey in a hammock on the beach. / All right, all right. All right.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein needs to tell Ben and Leslie to relax after the triplets news.
jokes.punchline: He describes relaxation through absurdly specific celebrity/cultural references, and Ben's 'All right, all right. All right' is the perfect McConaughey impression callback.
jokes.explanation: A two-part joke that escalates beautifully. 'Buddha on quaaludes' is a great absurd image, but 'Matthew McConaughey in a hammock on the beach' sets up Ben's involuntary McConaughey impression ('All right, all right. All right.') which is the real payoff. The structure is near-perfect — doctor delivers the image, Ben enacts it without meaning to. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Triplets? That's wonderful news. I had quadruplets with my third wife. Well, technically my fourth wife had them, but I was there for most of it.

jokes.text: I just multiplied all our future expenses by three, and you know what happened? The numbers got a lot higher. I think I heard the computer laugh at me.
jokes.setup: Ben, an accountant, is processing the financial reality of triplets.
jokes.punchline: His accounting instincts have kicked in, but his delivery — 'the numbers got a lot higher,' as if this is a surprise finding — and the absurdist touch of the computer laughing at him make this land.
jokes.explanation: Strong Ben joke that uses his accounting character to process the emotional news. 'The numbers got a lot higher' is deliberately obvious (tautological) in a way that captures shell-shocked thinking. 'I think I heard the computer laugh at me' is a good absurdist cap.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're having triplets! That's three future city council members, three future state senators, and one future president. I'm thinking two of them run for president in 2052, they split the vote, and the third one becomes Supreme Court Justice and settles it.

jokes.text: Are you ready to go, my gentle dove? / Oh, I will be there in two flaps of a butterfly's wing, and I love you.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are performing exaggerated calm for the doctor's benefit after receiving life-altering news.
jokes.punchline: Both deliver over-the-top serene endearments while clearly holding back existential panic.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of performing calm while clearly not feeling it. 'Two flaps of a butterfly's wing' is a lovely absurd escalation of the 'gentle dove' register. Both characters committing to the bit while barely holding it together is good ensemble work.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: As women age, their ovaries release multiple eggs as a sort of biological clearance event. It's like when a store realizes it's stuck with merchandise nobody wants, so they just put everything on sale at once.

jokes.text: We are so [bleep] screwed.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have been performing extreme calm and endearment for the doctor.
jokes.punchline: The moment they're alone, Ben's facade breaks and he delivers the honest assessment in stark contrast.
jokes.explanation: The comedic release after the performed calm. Not the most original joke structurally (facade drops, true feelings emerge) but executed with good economy and timing. The bleep adds a small bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I... I don't... we're having... Leslie's pregnant. With triplets. I can't... what do I... how do you even... there's three of them. Three babies. At the same time. I'm not... I've never... oh God.

jokes.text: Uh-oh. What did you do now, Joe? — Donna sees Joe comforting a crying woman and assumes the worst.
jokes.setup: Donna hears crying and sees Joe in a consoling scene.
jokes.punchline: She immediately assumes Joe is the cause of someone's distress — establishing her view of him as a relational hazard — but it turns out he found a lost dog.
jokes.explanation: A setup for the misdirection that follows — Donna assumes Joe caused harm, making the reveal of his kindness funnier. Functions well as a scene-entry joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: You need complete rest and to avoid all stress.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Think of stress like a celebrity—you need to avoid it like it's Lindsay Lohan in 2007.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: And relaxation? Relaxation is like heroin. You want more and more of it, and eventually it'll kill you.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Actually, scratch that—relaxation is like a non-lethal heroin. A completely safe heroin with no side effects that also cures cancer.

jokes.text: Joe spent six hours driving around looking for a student's lost dog, made muffins last night, and offers them to the family.
jokes.setup: Donna has warned Ron that Joe is her 'Tammy' — a dangerous, destabilizing presence.
jokes.punchline: Joe's 'danger' is that he is relentlessly, almost intimidatingly kind — he spent six hours finding a lost dog and made fresh muffins.
jokes.explanation: The inverted danger-man joke — the person framed as a destructive force is simply a devoted, thoughtful human being. Works because Donna's fear of him is genuinely character-based: she's afraid of being 'tamed' by goodness.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Matthew McConaughey

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Alright, alright, alright.

jokes.text: Oh, who knows? I got so many kids from different women, I just get all of their birthdays out of the way one day a year.
jokes.setup: At a party, someone asks whose birthday it is.
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals he has children with multiple women and has consolidated all birthdays into a single annual event for efficiency.
jokes.explanation: Solid Tom joke. The efficiency angle ('get them all out of the way') for something that should be a personal milestone is very Tom. The 'different women' detail adds to his character's comedic bachelorhood mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do you know what three times anything is? It's three of that thing! Three times the diapers, three times the formula, three times the tiny clothes that they grow out of in like five minutes!

jokes.text: It's about Larry. He is very sick. He has some kind of disease. / Oh, so that's why you've been so nice to him and let him carry all your stuff. / Yes, that's the reason. Good call, babe.
jokes.setup: Under pressure, Andy invents a cover story about Larry being sick to explain his weird behavior.
jokes.punchline: April immediately accepts this and retroactively justifies Andy's behavior — and Andy goes along with her conclusion that he was being nice to Larry as an act of pity, when really he was exploiting Larry.
jokes.explanation: The 'Good call, babe' is perfectly Andy — he smoothly adopts her interpretation as his own retroactive justification. The subtext that he was actually using Larry (letting him carry stuff) makes it darker and funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so if we liquidate our savings, sell the house, and I start a underground poker game in the basement, we could be solvent by... oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you hear that? The computer just made that beeping sound. That's the IRS. They're in the walls.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And that whirring noise? That's them accessing my browser history. I knew I shouldn't have Googled 'how to hide money legally.'

jokes.text: Leslie conducting the auction in an unnaturally calm, almost meditative state, starting bids at $40 for VIP passes.
jokes.setup: Leslie, who is usually a dynamo, has been instructed to stay calm and stress-free. She's running a charity auction.
jokes.punchline: The result is an agonizingly placid Leslie who speaks in hushed, zen tones and starts VIP concert passes at $40.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a high-energy character lobotomized by circumstance. Leslie's suppressed competitiveness leaking through in the form of terrible auction performance is a good sustained bit. 'We're all just calm and happy people enjoying ourselves together on earth' is a nice line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am ready. I am centered. I am one with the universe. Namaste.

jokes.text: I don't have the gavel, so I'm powerless. I respect the hierarchy of the auction!
jokes.setup: Tom points out that $50 for VIP passes is below face value and that Leslie needs more passion.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's explanation for why she can't do better reveals her entire psychology: she can't challenge the auctioneer's authority because there's a clear hierarchy and she must respect it.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's bureaucratic reverence for procedural hierarchy, even when she's the one being hurt by it, is a great character joke. 'I respect the hierarchy of the auction!' delivered with genuine conviction is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm centered. I'm calm. I'm at peace with the universe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what day is it? Oh my God, the city council meeting is tomorrow! I haven't prepared my three binders!

jokes.text: Leslie is already the queen of stress, so I have to be like her stress shamwow. I wrap myself around her, I soak up all of her stress, and then after the kids are born, someone can squeeze me out into a bucket.
jokes.setup: Ben is in a talking-head explaining his strategy for keeping Leslie calm.
jokes.punchline: The Shamwow metaphor, committed to in full detail including the 'squeeze me out into a bucket' image, is both surprisingly apt and gloriously absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Shamwow metaphor is unexpected and perfectly extended — the commitment to the bit with 'squeeze me out into a bucket' elevates it from a throwaway comparison to a fully realized comedic image. It also works on a character level: Ben sacrificing himself to absorb Leslie's stress is both funny and sweet. Highly quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: I found the student's lost dog by searching the neighborhood for six hours.

jokes.text: Ron! Ron, play with us! — Ron's daughters interrupt his woodworking with sharp tools to demand playtime.
jokes.setup: Ron has just sent a veiled threat to Joe ('tread lightly') and returned to serious woodworking.
jokes.punchline: Ron's daughters (named after plants, befitting his outdoorsy stoicism) squeal for him to play — visual comedy of Ron holding dangerous tools being besieged by small children.
jokes.explanation: Visual comedy of the imposing Ron being entirely at the mercy of small children. The 'Girls, Ron's got sharp tools now' line is a good straight delivery. Functions as setup for the song gag that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, it's nobody's birthday. I just combine them all into one party to save money. Much more efficient.

jokes.text: ♪ Eyes are watching, ears are listening / lips are closed, hands are still ♪ — Ron leads children in a classroom song to control them.
jokes.setup: Ron needs the kids to sit still and pay attention.
jokes.punchline: Joe leads a classroom management song, and the whole class (including Ron) falls into the ritual. Ron being implicitly controlled by the same technique meant for children is the visual joke.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of adult authority being puppeted by a children's song. Ron's grudging participation and the transition to him nodding approvingly ('that was well played') adds character depth to what could be a cheap sight gag.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We've got a party at the Sweetums factory at 2, then we need to swing by the car wash at 3, then we're catering the Rotary Club dinner at 5.

jokes.text: That was well played. Children their age respond positively to melody and rhyme.
jokes.setup: Joe has used a song to control the children, including Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron's grudging, analytical approval of the technique — delivered as if filing a tactical assessment — reveals he was won over against his will.
jokes.explanation: Ron's reluctant admiration for Joe's competence, delivered in his characteristic tactical register, is a nice character beat. 'That was well played' as a compliment to a classroom song is good deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I have something I need to tell you. It's about Larry.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What about him?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I found out that Larry... he's not actually from here. I mean, he is, but he wasn't always. And also, I think he might be involved in something. Something big.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that makes no sense.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know! That's how you know it's true!

jokes.text: Thirsty there, big guy? — Joe offers Ron a drink; reaction beat as Ron takes it while in a clearly suspicious state.
jokes.setup: Ron has just had a moment of connection with Joe over woodworking but is still on guard.
jokes.punchline: Joe's casual offer and Ron's 'Well, jeez, yes. Thank you so much' — an unusually warm response from Ron — signals his defenses are crumbling.
jokes.explanation: A transitional beat in Ron's arc. The comedy is in Ron's warmth breaking through ('Well, jeez, yes. Thank you so much' is unusually effusive for him). Serves the scene more than it stands alone.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's not being nice to Larry. He's just grateful that Larry's finally giving him an excuse to stop pretending to like him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thank you, Larry. Thank you so much.

jokes.text: Do you remember the time when you put sleeping pills in my soda? I fell right over in the middle of a town hall meeting. / Mm, no. I don't remember that. / You made a video of it and showed it at my birthday party. / Yes, it went over really big.
jokes.setup: Donna is confronting Joe about past bad behavior while Ron watches.
jokes.punchline: Joe's selective memory ('Mm, no') of drugging her in public — then his admission that he made a video and showed it at her birthday — delivered with cheerful nostalgia, escalates the horror while maintaining his warm exterior.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The escalation structure is perfect: (1) drugging someone is bad → (2) he denies it → (3) she proves it with the video → (4) his pride in the video's reception ('it went over really big') recontextualizes his warmth as something more sinister. Explains why Donna fears him despite his surface charm. Highly quotable and surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, we're starting the bidding for VIP passes to the Harvest Festival at just $5!

dialogue.speaker: Auctioneer
dialogue.line: Do I hear $5? Going once...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. $5 is insulting. These passes are worth at least $500!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't change the starting bid mid-auction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. But I'm bidding $500 myself.

jokes.text: Yeah, um, I have got an itch that I have not been able to get to all day, and even against the wall, nothing will do it. Would you mind doing that? — Joe scratches Donna's back.
jokes.setup: Joe says 'Is there anything I can do to make it up to you?' after apologizing for the sleeping pill incident.
jokes.punchline: Donna's 'making it up to her' turns out to be a very mundane back scratch — but the oversharing detail about trying the wall makes it funnier, and Joe instantly and cheerfully complies.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of Joe's apology for drugging someone being accepted as a back scratch is funny. Donna's detailed description of her failed scratch attempts is an overshare that adds to her character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm just going to breathe. In through my nose, out through my mouth. The auction is just energy, and energy is neither created nor destroyed, it's only transformed. So if I transform my anxiety into positive chi, then...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're hyperventilating.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's just my body's way of saying hello to the universe.

jokes.text: Andy, you can say 'Okay.' / Okay. Bye. / I didn't mean to say 'Bye.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Andy to keep the secret and just say 'Okay.' Andy says 'Okay' then involuntarily adds 'Bye.'
jokes.punchline: Andy's confused correction of his own goodbye — 'I didn't mean to say Bye' — is a small perfect character beat. He said it because he panicked.
jokes.explanation: A tiny, perfectly crafted beat. The involuntary 'Bye' followed by Andy's embarrassed clarification reveals his anxiety through action rather than statement. Economical, character-specific, and surprisingly quotable. 'I didn't mean to say Bye' has an Andy-ness that elevates it above a simple reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was following proper auction protocol. You need to file a Form 27-B with the Parks Department at least 72 hours before any vocal projection over 85 decibels.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not a real form.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It is now. I'm making it real right now.

jokes.text: A very wealthy and elegant-looking woman with a diamond-encrusted eye patch just raised her hand. Don't look at her. She doesn't like attention, but she's there. She's real.
jokes.setup: The auction is going badly; Leslie, suppressed by doctor's orders, tries to generate excitement.
jokes.punchline: She invents a fictional bidder in extraordinarily specific, vivid terms — 'diamond-encrusted eye patch' — and her insistence that this person is real ('She's real') while calmly asking people not to look is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Leslie inventing a fictional auction bidder with a 'diamond-encrusted eye patch' is a delightful absurdist departure. The escalation of detail ('She doesn't like attention, but she's there. She's real.') as she tries to sell this lie under enforced calm is brilliant. The insistence on reality ('She's real') is the perfect deadpan commitment to the bit. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: The sheik has thrown his hat into the ring. / There's no sheik. / With the crazy hat and a monkey on his shoulder. / There's no bidding war. No one's talking... / There's no sheik, and there's no old lady with a diamond—what is it, a diamond eye patch?
jokes.setup: Leslie has invented a fictional diamond-eye-patch bidder; now she doubles down by inventing a second fictional bidder.
jokes.punchline: Tom's increasingly exasperated attempts to shut this down ('There's no sheik') as Leslie escalates the fiction with a monkey detail is the core joke, capped by Tom's 'what is it, a diamond eye patch?' showing even he's absorbed the original detail.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the fictional auction bidders joke. Leslie adding a sheik with a crazy hat and monkey pushes the absurdism further. Tom's callback to the eye patch detail ('what is it, a diamond eye patch?') shows the earlier joke has lodged in everyone's brain, including the person arguing against it. Strong ensemble back-and-forth.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: You see, Ron, the key to a perfect joint is to ensure your wood grain is running in the same direction as your—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: —chisel blade. Yes, I'm aware.

dialogue.speaker: Both
dialogue.line: It's basic carpentry.

jokes.text: Naming rights for the kids' tent go to Jamm Orthodontics for 100 smackers. Now that is the steal of the day.
jokes.setup: After the entire fictional bidder debacle, the item sells for $100 to the only real bidder.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's Zen-calm acceptance of a terrible outcome, calling it 'the steal of the day,' is the perfect defeated-but-serene closer.
jokes.explanation: Good capper to the auction scene. 'The steal of the day' delivered with genuine-sounding enthusiasm for a disastrous outcome is a solid ironic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Remember when we used to slip a little something into the punch at those office parties?

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Those were the days.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Nobody ever suspected a thing. Good times.

jokes.text: So, um, Andy told me what's going on. / Really? Oh. I was trying to keep it hush-hush. It's kind of embarrassing.
jokes.setup: April approaches Larry saying Andy told her his secret. Larry thinks Andy revealed the pregnancy.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response — 'it's kind of embarrassing' — about what he thinks is being discussed sets up the misdirection that Andy told April something else entirely.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the swallowed wedding ring reveal. The misdirection is well-managed — both April and the audience assume Andy revealed the pregnancy, making the actual reveal more surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Joe drugged me. The additional humiliation of public screening.

jokes.text: Well, earlier today, I was licking icing off of my finger, and then, boom, I swallow my wedding ring. And I wish I could say it was the first time, but— / Wait, wait, wait. So you're not, like, dying?
jokes.setup: April thinks she's been told Larry has a serious illness.
jokes.punchline: Larry reveals he swallowed his wedding ring — again, apparently, as 'I wish I could say it was the first time' lands as a casually horrifying escalation. April's 'So you're not, like, dying?' is the perfect deflated reaction.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Larry joke. 'I wish I could say it was the first time' is the real gem — casually implying this is a recurring problem for Larry is deeply funny and perfectly characterizes his hapless dignity. The misdirection payoff (illness → ring swallowing) is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: How can I make up for past behavior?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You can start by giving me a foot massage.

jokes.text: I've gotten very good at passing it. It's just a matter of getting out the old colander.
jokes.setup: April asks if swallowing the wedding ring is painful.
jokes.punchline: Larry's matter-of-fact description of his recovery process — 'getting out the old colander' — delivered with cheerful competence, is the dark escalation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Getting out the old colander' is a brilliant dark comedy image — the casual domesticity of using a colander for this purpose, the implied 'old' colander (dedicated to this task?), and Larry's matter-of-fact expertise. The economy is outstanding. Comparable to and arguably above the 8.0 anchor in terms of shock and specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, imagine this: A mysterious billionaire walks in. He's tall, handsome, drives a Tesla. He's never heard of Parks and Recreation, so he has no idea what he's bidding on, but he doesn't care because he's SO rich. He sees the gazebo and he goes, 'I'll pay a million dollars.' Just like that. A million dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And then his even richer brother walks in and says, 'I'll pay TWO million dollars,' and they get into this bidding war, and by the end they've raised fifty million dollars for the Parks Department, and they're so grateful they both want to name their children after me.

jokes.text: Come on, Pearl, jump in. Don't make me pull the permits on your rental units. / Hey, all the paperwork on those buildings are under my dog's name, so if you got a problem, take it up with Princess.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to raise auction bids for the Red Hot Chili Peppers guitar.
jokes.punchline: Pearl casually reveals she's hiding rental property under her dog's name, threatening to escalate this to 'Princess' for negotiations — an absurdly elaborate and illegal workaround from a presumably elderly bidder.
jokes.explanation: A very funny aside. The specificity of the con ('under my dog's name') and the proud escalation ('take it up with Princess') from what should be a minor auction extra is delightfully absurd. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so we also have a bid from the Sweetums Corporation... no wait, that's real. Um, we have a bid from... Reggie Philbin's cousin, Derek Philbin. He's very interested in the park.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And then there's also Congressman Jam's investment group, 'Jam Enterprises.' They're prepared to offer... I'm making this up, aren't I?

jokes.text: Guys, come on, now. This is signed by the Red Hot Chili Peppers. Just think about all their great songs, covering everything from the culture of Southern California to drug use in Southern California.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to talk up the RHCP guitar to generate bids.
jokes.punchline: His attempt to describe the band's range ends up revealing that their range is, essentially, two overlapping themes about Southern California.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke. The structure of 'everything from X to Y' where X and Y are nearly identical is a classic deadpan pattern, but the specificity (Southern California culture / drug use in Southern California) makes it feel fresh. Good characterization of Ben as a slightly square music appreciator.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have a bid of $50,000 from a gentleman in the back.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Now $75,000 from a very attractive woman who just walked in.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And we have $100,000 from a man who appears to be made entirely of money.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: $125,000 from a mysterious billionaire who communicates only through interpretive dance.

jokes.text: Why would you erase the signatures? / I'm more of a Jack Johnson guy.
jokes.setup: An auction-goer (Herman) has apparently erased the RHCP signatures from the guitar.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm more of a Jack Johnson guy' — an utterly calm and non-apologetic explanation for a piece of vandalism/theft at a charity auction.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. Five words that explain absolutely nothing while explaining everything about Herman's character. The calmness of 'I'm more of a Jack Johnson guy' as a complete justification for destroying charity auction property is absurdly funny. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: April, I need to tell you something embarrassing that happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was at the grocery store and I tripped in the produce section and fell into a display of watermelons.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dude, Larry didn't just fall — he LAUNCHED himself through the air like a heat-seeking missile and demolished an entire pyramid of watermelons. People were screaming. A child cried. Security had to be called.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I tripped and knocked over maybe three watermelons.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It was the most catastrophic produce incident since the great cantaloupe shortage of '09.

jokes.text: Ben cuts his hand on the guitar strings during the struggle; blood everywhere; Leslie screams for a doctor, then a coroner.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to get the guitar back from Herman.
jokes.punchline: The struggle results in Ben cutting his hand. Leslie, in full panic-suppressed mode, screams 'Call a doctor! No, call a coroner!' — her anxiety escalating straight past triage to obituary.
jokes.explanation: The slapstick (Ben cutting his hand on guitar strings) is fine, but the real joke is Leslie's catastrophizing — going from 'call a doctor' to 'call a coroner' in one breath is a great character beat showing her suppressed anxiety breaking through.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So I swallowed my wedding ring. The doctor said I'd have to wait for nature to take its course. My wife asked how I was going to get it back, and I said, 'Well, I guess we'll just have to see what comes out.' She didn't think that was funny.

jokes.text: You have very weak hands. / Why would you say that?
jokes.setup: Ben has just cut his hand and is presumably in some pain.
jokes.punchline: Herman's immediate, unprompted assessment of Ben's hand strength as the cause of the injury — delivered with complete seriousness — is a wonderful character flourish.
jokes.explanation: Herman is turning into a great one-episode character. His lack of self-awareness about his role in the injury, combined with an unprompted critique, is excellent deadpan. 'Why would you say that?' from Ben is the ideal straight response.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The Red Hot Chili Peppers have written approximately 200 songs about California, socks, and the lyrics 'funky monkey' repeated over and over.

jokes.text: You know the EMT said that if flea had sent you his bass, you could've lost a thumb.
jokes.setup: Ben insists he's fine after cutting his hand at the auction.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reassurance accidentally becomes a worst-case-scenario elaboration — apparently the EMT provided a detailed counterfactual about a bass guitar and thumb amputation.
jokes.explanation: Good dark Leslie joke. The specificity of 'Flea's bass' and 'lost a thumb' — framed as comforting — is exactly Leslie's kind of anxious optimism. The EMT apparently volunteered this information unprompted, which adds an additional absurd layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, someone erased the Red Hot Chili Peppers signatures? Do you know how much that's worth? That's a collectible! That's like... that's like taking the Mona Lisa and drawing a mustache on it!

jokes.text: I'm totally fine, babe. Everything is a-okay coolio beans.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to perform calm for Leslie's benefit after his injury.
jokes.punchline: 'A-okay coolio beans' — Ben's attempt at casual reassurance produces an expression no adult has ever used unironically, revealing the strain beneath the performance.
jokes.explanation: 'Coolio beans' is a funny phrase that reveals Ben's Midwestern squareness and his awkward attempt to sound casual. Good character detail.

dialogue.speaker: Herman
dialogue.line: Look, I like what I like. The Red Hot Chili Peppers are okay, but they're not really my thing. I'm more of a Nickelback guy.

jokes.text: I wonder if I'll ever stop doing that. — Ann refers to the habit of calling Ann by name even though she's moved away.
jokes.setup: Leslie instinctively calls out 'Ann?' when she needs medical help, then remembers Ann no longer works there.
jokes.punchline: Her resigned self-commentary — 'I wonder if I'll ever stop doing that' — makes her habit both funny and touching.
jokes.explanation: A recurring season 6 beat made poignant by Leslie's genuine attachment to Ann. 'I wonder if I'll ever stop doing that' is a funny/sad line that characterizes Leslie's loyalty well.

dialogue.speaker: Herman
dialogue.line: Look, those signatures were in ballpoint pen. Ballpoint! Do you know what kind of ink degradation we're talking about here? In fifty years, those signatures would be completely illegible. I was doing a public service.

dialogue.speaker: Herman
dialogue.line: Plus, the signatures were crowding the album cover. The negative space was completely unbalanced. It's called composition, people.

jokes.text: When we're together, all we do is have sex, sit on the couch, eat homemade pasta, have sex again. He's constantly being respectful, wanting to spend time with me, trying to 'connect' with me. It's a nightmare. I become boring.
jokes.setup: Ron asks why Donna finds Joe dangerous given that he seems to be a good person.
jokes.punchline: Donna's 'nightmare' of a relationship is described as: sex, homemade pasta, sex, respect, and emotional connection. Her delivery of 'connect' in scare quotes and 'I become boring' reveals that she equates stability with personal death.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. The inversion — framing an ideal relationship as a horror — is the core joke, but the specific items in the list (homemade pasta sandwiched between sex, 'connect' in air quotes, 'I become boring') are exactly right. 'It's a nightmare. I become boring.' is the perfect punchline. Total Donna. Comparable to or above the 8.0 anchor in character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Herman
dialogue.line: Well, the good news is you're going to live. The bad news is you're still you.

jokes.text: Live your life how you want, but don't confuse drama with happiness.
jokes.setup: Ron, the man who has been married to two women named Tammy, tells Donna not to mistake drama for happiness.
jokes.punchline: The irony that Ron — whose love life is essentially a Greek tragedy — is delivering relationship wisdom is the joke. But it lands as both funny AND genuinely insightful.
jokes.explanation: Quietly excellent. The line is genuinely wise, but coming from Ron — who has had two Tammys, been declared legally dead for a plane ticket, and yet still operates this way — it's a layered joke. The character integration is exceptional because Ron has EARNED this advice through suffering. Highly quotable as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're going to be fine. At least you didn't get hit by a blimp.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A blimp?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, a blimp could've hit you. Then you'd really be in trouble.

jokes.text: Technically, we're all dying, unless you choose the right grail. It's the dusty one.
jokes.setup: April is told that Larry isn't dying, just swallowed his ring.
jokes.punchline: Andy's philosophical pivot — 'technically we're all dying' — escalated by a completely serious Indiana Jones Holy Grail reference as existential life advice.
jokes.explanation: Lovely Andy absurdism. The pivot from existential truth to Indiana Jones lore ('the dusty one') as if this is actionable life advice is exactly his kind of earnest surrealism. 'It's the dusty one' delivered as genuine guidance is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Joe is my Tammy because he's successful, he's handsome, he's well-dressed, he makes a lot of money, and he's extremely organized.

jokes.text: Andy's escalating fake secrets: Ben's dog is dying / Ben is dying — he has the same disease Larry has / Leslie is dying / They're both dying / I'm dying / Chris and Ann are moving / They're moving again to China...town in France.
jokes.setup: April demands Andy tell her the real secret. He invents increasingly desperate lies.
jokes.punchline: Each lie is worse than the last, culminating in 'Chinatown in France' — a place that doesn't exist, delivered as a confident revelation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating absurdist sequence. Each fake secret is worse ('Ben is dying,' 'Leslie is dying,' 'I'm dying') and then the pivot to 'Chinatown in France' is a perfect non-sequitur escalation beyond death. The structure of April shooting each one down with a flat 'No' and Andy persisting makes the rhythm perfect. 'Chinatown in France' specifically is a great coinage.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Joe makes me happy. We have a great relationship. He's kind, he's thoughtful, he listens to me.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: And honestly, it scares me to death.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm becoming a normal person with normal problems and a normal relationship. What is happening to me?

jokes.text: Joe notices Ron's rear tire is flat and proactively patches it, then mentions Ron should still go to a garage.
jokes.setup: Ron is already being grudgingly charmed by Joe's competence.
jokes.punchline: Joe has gone out of his way to fix Ron's tire without being asked, then immediately discloses the limits of his fix ('you're still gonna want to go to a garage') — characterizing him as both helpful and honest. The joke is that his 'flaw' makes him even more perfect.
jokes.explanation: Part of the Joe-is-impossibly-perfect running gag. The tire fix followed by an honest disclosure of its limits is a small beat in the Ron/Joe arc.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You just described every relationship I've ever had.

jokes.text: I'll wear that red thing when you deserve to see me in that red thing.
jokes.setup: Joe asks Donna to wear 'that red thing' to their upcoming dinner.
jokes.punchline: Donna's reframe — it's not a refusal, it's a conditional with an implied power dynamic — is a great character line that establishes her control of the relationship.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Donna line. The conditional construction ('when you deserve to see me in that red thing') accomplishes multiple things: establishes her power, maintains allure, and delivers a joke through pure confidence and economy. The parallel structure of the sentence is flawless. Highly quotable and entirely Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I have a secret. I think... I think Austria and Australia are the same place.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They're not.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Really? Because I've been saying it wrong my whole life.

jokes.text: [Clears throat] Gotta go make some muffins.
jokes.setup: Joe and Donna have just had a charged exchange. The moment is almost romantic.
jokes.punchline: Joe breaks the tension with 'Gotta go make some muffins' — an absurdly domestic non-sequitur that both deflates the moment and confirms his wholesome domesticity.
jokes.explanation: The muffins callback as a romantic deflation device is very effective. 'Gotta go make some muffins' is a perfect line — domestic, specific, slightly absurd as a mic-drop exit. The callback to the earlier muffin moment reinforces Joe's character.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: I noticed your car's oil was looking a little dark, so I went ahead and changed it for you. Also rotated your tires, replaced your air filter, and detailed the interior. No need to thank me!

jokes.text: I mean, hey, you're looking at a woman who just hit triple cherries in her uterus.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are discussing how they'll raise money for the concert, and Leslie mentions the lottery.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's metaphor for having triplets — 'triple cherries in her uterus' — is a gleefully absurd slot machine analogy that captures her characteristic framing of everything as an achievement.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Triple cherries in her uterus' is an inspired metaphor — specific, visual, and characteristically Leslie in framing biological luck as a kind of victory. The slot machine image applied to the uterus is fresh and memorable. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Babe, our kids will be geniuses. They'll get scholarships. Half of my tuition was paid for by the Indiana scholarship for pretty blondes who like to read. It's now called the Virginia Woolf prize—different time.
jokes.setup: Ben is panicking about the cost of raising triplets. Leslie tries to reassure him they'll get scholarships.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals she benefited from a scholarship for 'pretty blondes who like to read' — its current rebranding as the Virginia Woolf prize and her 'different time' acknowledge both the sexism and her breezy acceptance of having benefited from it.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The 'Indiana scholarship for pretty blondes who like to read' is a great absurdist institution, and the rename to 'Virginia Woolf prize' is a perfect satirical note — both acknowledging the sexism and showing that Leslie has no self-awareness about having benefited from it ('different time' as a casual dismissal). Character-specific, original, quotable, and layered.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If we win the lottery, we could have triplets!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, the odds of winning the lottery are like one in 175 million.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So you're saying there's a chance? Because having triplets is basically hitting the jackpot. Cha-ching!

jokes.text: We spent too much money on macaroons. / Okay, wait, what's the number for the Louvre? I mean, maybe I can get a refund. We barely looked at the Mona Lisa.
jokes.setup: Ben reveals they spent their entire savings on a Paris trip and is now panicking about triplet expenses.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is to call the Louvre to try to get a refund for barely looking at the Mona Lisa — her crisis management approach is to treat a museum like a store with a return policy.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's problem-solving instinct applied to an impossible situation ('get a refund from the Louvre') is wonderful. 'We barely looked at the Mona Lisa' as grounds for a partial refund is absurdly logical from inside Leslie's brain.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our kids are going to get scholarships. I'm talking about academic scholarships, athletic scholarships, and scholarships for having really good penmanship.

jokes.text: I'm shamwowing all of your stress, and there's no one here to wring me out.
jokes.setup: Ben had earlier described himself as Leslie's 'stress shamwow.' Now he is visibly breaking under the combined stress.
jokes.punchline: The callback to his own metaphor — 'there's no one here to wring me out' — is both a funny extension of the bit and a genuine moment of vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: The shamwow callback works as both comedy and character revelation. Ben's system — absorbing Leslie's stress — has been overwhelmed, and his articulation of it through the same metaphor is structurally satisfying. 'There's no one here to wring me out' is a perfect extension of the original image.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we spent HOW much on that baguette warmer?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It was in the shape of the Eiffel Tower, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That doesn't make it a necessary purchase!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You said, and I quote, 'Every baguette deserves to be warm and patriotic.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was in PARIS, Ben. I was emotionally compromised!

jokes.text: You just look so crazy right now, but cute. You're always stressed out. How are you calm right now?
jokes.setup: Ben has been spiraling in financial panic. Leslie, who is usually the anxious one, finds herself calm.
jokes.punchline: Leslie observing that Ben 'looks so crazy right now, but cute' — the role reversal complete — is a funny inversion of their usual dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Decent character comedy. The reversal of who's calm and who's panicking is the joke, and Leslie's observation is sweet and funny. Not exceptional but works well in the emotional arc.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I realized that worrying doesn't help anything. I'm just going to focus on the things I can control and let go of the things I can't. It's actually very freeing.

jokes.text: Leslie's immunity-to-stress speech ending with 'Larry changing his name for some stupid reason' in her list of challenges
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering a heartfelt speech about how their shared experiences have prepared them for this
jokes.punchline: The list includes serious things (harvest festival, recall, Ann leaving) and then 'Larry changing his name for some stupid reason' — the mundane Larry complaint inserted into a list of genuine hardships
jokes.explanation: A good list joke — the insertion of a petty complaint about Larry into a serious emotional speech is perfectly timed. The word 'stupid' shows Leslie still hasn't made peace with it. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Once upon a time, there was a brave knight named Sir Ronald of Swanson, who slayed dragons with his bare hands and built his own castle out of wood he personally harvested.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: That's not a real fairy tale!

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's called 'The Woodworker and the Eggplant Parmesan.' It's a classic.

jokes.text: Ron is King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest. / Much obliged. — Ron wearing a glittery crown bestowed by the children.
jokes.setup: Ron has been playing with the girls at the school.
jokes.punchline: Ron — the hyper-masculine, anti-government libertarian — is wearing a glittery crown and accepting the title 'King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest' with complete dignity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best jokes. 'King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest' is the single best name that could be assigned to Ron Swanson by children, and his 'Much obliged' — dignified, serious acceptance of this title — is perfect. The visual of Ron in a glittery crown with full gravitas is exceptional. The character integration score of 9.5 is earned: the joke works ONLY for Ron. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? I think Ron has actually grown as a person. He's become more open, more collaborative, more human.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Thank you, Donna. That means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah. You're basically a 'Sensitive Government Warrior' now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to pretend you didn't say that.

jokes.text: Did you think even two years ago you'd be playing matchmaker for me while wearing a glittery crown? Now you're a dad. You care a little, itty bit about your friends. You're King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest. It suits you.
jokes.setup: Donna is reflecting on how much Ron has changed since becoming a stepdad.
jokes.punchline: The callback to 'King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest' as the summation of Ron's character growth — framed as a compliment — lands because it's both absurd and emotionally true.
jokes.explanation: The callback elevates the original joke. 'It suits you' applied to 'King Sparkle of Cupcake Forest' as a description of Ron's emotional growth is both funny and genuinely touching. Works as comedy because of the juxtaposition; works as drama because it's true. Strong character integration for Ron's arc this season.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're pregnant! April and I are gonna have a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I did it. I accomplished something. Me. Andy Dwyer.

jokes.text: Babe, you don't have to hide from me. I don't care about the secret anymore. / ...But screw it. You're more important than anything. I'm gonna tell you 'cause it's super juicy — you ready?
jokes.setup: April gives Andy a genuine, heartfelt speech about trust in their marriage — she no longer needs the secret.
jokes.punchline: Andy's response to this profound display of trust is to tell her anyway because it's 'super juicy' — completely missing the emotional point while proving his character.
jokes.explanation: Good Andy beat. The emotional moment of April's genuine trust speech is immediately deflated by Andy's mercenary 'it's super juicy' pivot. He's not motivated by trust — he's motivated by having a good secret to share. Very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Congratulations on your child. I'm sure it will be a fine human being. But mark my words, Leslie, Ben... that child will disagree with you. And when it does, I will be there... to agree with the child.

jokes.text: Everybody, if you could gather around... / They're here — don't try to get it out of me anymore. / The reason I have been acting so weird is not because I've been waiting for the results of the soil samples to come back. / Well, jeez, I've been up all night trying to make sure— / It doesn't matter, Larry. It was a pointless ruse designed to waste time.
jokes.setup: Andy is about to reveal the pregnancy. He performs a fake-out about soil samples.
jokes.punchline: Larry, who has apparently taken the soil sample ruse seriously and stayed up all night working on it, is immediately dismissed by Andy ('It was a pointless ruse designed to waste time').
jokes.explanation: Larry getting pulled into a totally fake cover story and doing real work overnight, only to be instantly dismissed, is perfect Larry comedy. 'It was a pointless ruse designed to waste time' is a very funny delivery — honest in a way that's devastating to Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: This is great news for Leslie and Ben, but let's talk about what this means for me. I'm going to be the best godfather ever. Actually, I'm going to be better than a godfather. I'm going to be a god-uncle. That's a thing I just made up and it's trademarked.

jokes.text: Yes, I did it! I kept a secret.
jokes.setup: Andy has just revealed the pregnancy to the whole office.
jokes.punchline: His immediate self-congratulation — 'I kept a secret' — over a secret he barely kept, and which he literally just ended, is a wonderful beat of misplaced pride.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire Andy/secret running gag. His pride in having kept the secret for a few days — despite nearly cracking constantly — is perfectly Andy-brained self-assessment. Good economy.

jokes.text: Congratulations. I'm sure you will both raise a wonderful child with whom I will profoundly disagree on nearly everything.
jokes.setup: Everyone is celebrating the pregnancy announcement.
jokes.punchline: Ron's congratulations come with an immediate qualifier — he already anticipates ideological disagreement with the unborn children.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron joke that is simultaneously warm and entirely in character. He CAN'T just say 'congratulations' — he must immediately note that he'll disagree with the children's values (presumably because they'll be raised by Leslie, a government employee who believes in things). The specificity of 'on nearly everything' suggests he's given this real thought. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Well, actually, and this is crazy, but it's children, plural. We're having triplets, and... / Shut the— / Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: Ron has just congratulated them for a wonderful 'child.' Leslie corrects him.
jokes.punchline: April's 'Shut the—' (bleeped) and Tom's 'Oh, my God!' are the perfect ensemble reaction to the triplets reveal for a second time.
jokes.explanation: The secondary reveal of triplets to the office group is effective. April's bleeped reaction is the best beat. The structure mirrors the doctor's reveal but in a more intimate context.

jokes.text: Babe, I am so glad you didn't tell me. / I know. I'm incredible.
jokes.setup: April is reacting to the triplets news with joy.
jokes.punchline: Andy's response to April's appreciation is not humble but an immediate and sincere self-assessment: 'I know. I'm incredible.'
jokes.explanation: Good Andy beat. His genuine, non-ironic self-praise ('I know. I'm incredible.') for barely managing to keep a secret for a few days is perfect character work. Great economy.

jokes.text: A triple crib — sounds like an interesting woodworking challenge. Would you like oak or pine? I'll make both, and you can choose.
jokes.setup: The group is offering practical help to Leslie and Ben for the triplets.
jokes.punchline: Ron's expression of love and support is entirely through the offer of labor and material — he frames a crib as a 'woodworking challenge' and immediately doubles the offer because he can.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke with emotional warmth hidden inside craftsman pragmatism. 'Interesting woodworking challenge' as his way of saying 'I want to do something meaningful for you' is pure Ron. 'I'll make both, and you can choose' is the escalation — his affection expressed as doubled labor. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: My boyf— my friend Joe has the hookup at all the good preschools.
jokes.setup: Everyone is offering resources for the triplets. Donna offers Joe's preschool connections.
jokes.punchline: Donna starts to say 'my boyfriend' and self-corrects to 'my friend' — a tiny admission that things have shifted, caught mid-word.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire Donna/Joe arc. The slip of 'boyf-' is perfectly timed — Donna can't even complete the word before catching herself, but she's already revealed everything. Great economy and emotional resonance within a comedy beat.

jokes.text: Andy and I can babysit anytime, except for on weekends and nights, but we're free anytime during work hours.
jokes.setup: The group is offering to help with the triplets. April offers to babysit.
jokes.punchline: April's caveat — available anytime except weekends, nights, or basically any time one would actually need a babysitter — reduces the offer to worthlessness while she delivers it with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp April joke. The 'except for on weekends and nights' systematically eliminates every time one would need a babysitter, leaving only 'work hours' — when the parents are, by definition, not watching the children anyway. The sincerity of the offer makes it funnier. Good structure.

jokes.text: Well, I sold everything on the auction list, no thanks to you people. What's so wonderful that you're all celebrating while I do all the hard work? / We're having triplets. / [Laughter] Oh, great. First my cousin Winona gets into a car accident the night my one-man show opens, and now this? Why are my accomplishments always overshadowed? Congratulations, I suppose.
jokes.setup: Craig storms in, proud of having saved the auction, to find everyone celebrating something else.
jokes.punchline: Craig's response to the triplets news is to pivot to grievance — citing his cousin Winona's car accident on the opening night of his one-man show as a comparable injustice — and then grudgingly offer 'Congratulations, I suppose.'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Craig joke and a great episode closer (comedically). The structure is perfect: Craig does something genuinely helpful (sold everything) → learns about triplets → instead of celebrating, pivots to his own grievance → the grievance is perfectly calibrated (a COUSIN's car accident, not even his own, vs. a ONE-MAN SHOW) → 'Congratulations, I suppose' as a resigned acceptance. The specificity of Winona and 'one-man show' makes this exceptional. One of the episode's top-tier jokes.

jokes.text: Craig bursts in: 'First my cousin Winona gets into a car accident the night my one-man show opens, and now this? Why are my accomplishments always overshadowed? Congratulations, I suppose.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is celebrating Leslie's triplets announcement. Craig enters to announce he sold everything at the auction.
jokes.punchline: Craig's accomplishment (selling auction items) is overshadowed by triplets — he responds by making it about himself, comparing it to his cousin's car accident ruining his one-man show, then issuing a grudging 'Congratulations, I suppose'
jokes.explanation: A great Craig closer. The specificity of 'my cousin Winona gets into a car accident the night my one-man show opens' is perfect — Craig is the kind of person for whom these events are equally tragic. The false equivalence between a car accident and triplets, and his resentment of both, is excellent character comedy. 'Congratulations, I suppose' is one of the episode's best lines. Strong episode-ender joke.

tmdb_overview: Leslie, Ben, and Andy head to San Francisco for a National Parks Conference. Tom opens his restaurant, Ron has another run-in with his ex-wife Tammy 2, Andy lives a rock and roll fantasy, and Leslie makes a huge decision about her future.
insight: Jerry's incompetence reaches critical mass: 2.51 jokes per minute sustain the chaos.
